utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they have a very bad buzzing sound in the headphones and it's impossible to work that way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's gone now, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, it's not gone, it's still there in all the booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the deputy clerk attend to that. There is a sound. We'll wait for a minute or two to see whether it can be fixed. In the meantime, I should say that the approach towards punctuality has to be addressed. It's not right that the Judges should be outside at 9.00, waiting to come inside. In future, we will come in, whether the guard raps three times or not, when we're ready. The practice that is followed here is totally contrary to what is followed in domestic systems. We'll rise for ten minutes. --- Break taken at 9.08 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're ready to go now. So proceed with your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, yesterday we broke off when we were discussing the legality of police action. I'm going to quote point 19 to you, where it says: "The superior is responsible for the acts of his subordinates if he knew or had reason to know that his subordinates are preparing to commit such acts or have already committed such acts and the superior did not take indispensable, reasonable measures to punish the perpetrators -- to prevent such acts or punish the perpetrators." My question to you is: Did the police take measures to prevent any criminal acts, and did it take measures to punish the perpetrators if it found out about a crime that had been perpetrated?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While staying in Kosovo and Metohija and contacting many senior and mid-level officials, I personally saw that officials at all levels in the police structure did everything within their power to prevent illegal acts. If they did happen, they were documented. Every effort was made to resolve them, to find the perpetrators, and to hand them over to the appropriate organs of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any case when such action was not taken or, rather, when anybody got off easy?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that very clearly: I'm not aware of a single case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What would be the basis for your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I cannot hear any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll try again. What is the basis for the information that you just gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I asked what is the basis for the information that you just gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basis for the information that just -- that I just gave is what I tried to say during my introductory remarks: That I attended many important meetings at the level of the state leadership, at the level of the ministry, at top levels, and at the level of the staff of the Ministry of the Interior in Pristina. In addition to that, I had very frequent contacts with police officials at different levels, and I was assured through all of these contacts that they were all very insistent on this, that the police should act lawfully. Not ever did I get even a minimal impression that anybody was not acting in accordance with the law let alone that the police had a plan to act not in accordance with the law. Of course, to this I can add that there are many documents, and I hope that we will be able to look at them during the course of the day. These documents show what officials at different levels did and what kind of orders they gave to their subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you profess to have a knowledge that would cover every possible infraction by a soldier and a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, of course that is not what I'm professing. What I said a moment ago does not pertain to individual isolated cases. Of course there were some such cases, and of course measures were always taken whenever the police found out about any such case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, you say that you know of no case where action was not taken. Can I turn that question around and ask if you know of cases where action was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I know of such cases. There are many. Very quickly, I can remember at least a few such cases, and in our documentation there are certainly documents showing that the police did prosecute all criminal offences and anything else that was impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does your knowledge of such cases extend to cases where the police -- where action was taken against police officers for murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it does extend to such cases. Off-the-cuff, I can remember at least four or five such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the outcome of these cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do not know the ultimate outcome at this very moment, up to this very moment, but I certainly know that while the police were still in Kosovo each and every such case was dealt with to the very end as far as such cases are concerned; namely, the perpetrators were arrested, a criminal report was filed, and they were handed over, the perpetrators were handed over to the appropriate organs of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And were prosecuted where appropriate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quite certain that what was within the ambit of policework was done fully. As for procedure before the judiciary, I'm not aware of the details, especially because I was no longer in the MUP and since we withdrew from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to what you said, General, yesterday you indicated an overview in tab 76. On the last page of this overview are registered crimes with perpetrators known, perpetrators unknown, and then the number of resolved criminal cases. There are 12 -- or, rather, 18 policemen who had perpetrated crimes, and according to your records they were criminally prosecuted. Is that what you're saying in relation to the cases that Mr. Bonomy asked you about?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I found the right page, on the last page of this tab, under number 11, there is the number of perpetrators of criminal offences who were found. And below that, horizontally, we can see how many terrorists, how many policemen, how many members of the army of Yugoslavia and how many civilians out of the total number. It can be seen that the number of perpetrators of crimes that resulted in death in the category under "Policemen" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... translated as it has some bearing on the charges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are discussing the overview of security related incidents resulting in death that we analysed partially yesterday. On the last page, under number 11, we have the number of perpetrators of criminal offences who were found, that is to say offences resulting in death, and we have the different categories of perpetrators. I assume that column number 6 vertically pertains to the war period, and it is evident that the total number of perpetrators from the category of terrorists is 192, policemen 12; the category of members of the army of Yugoslavia also 12; the category of civilian persons, a total of 11. Of course, other measures follow as well: How many criminal reports were filed, how many reports as such were filed, along with the charges, in terms of resolving the particular criminal cases, then how many charges were filed with civilian investigation organs and how many with investigation organs of the VJ, the army of Yugoslavia. These are only cases that resulted in death. In other tables, there are statistics involving other criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can I take it it's not possible from this table to tell whether anyone was convicted and punished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Judge. That cannot be seen from this table because that is not within the remit of policework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say the police don't keep records of people who are convicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in principle they do keep such records, but that was not the aim of this particular table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're the man that should know whether policemen were convicted or not. Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do not know specifically what the outcome in court was. I know of one particular case that is underway right now in the district court in Prokuplje, if I remember correctly, against a -- against a group of members of the reserve force of the ministry. These persons killed several persons in the area of Podujevo during the war. That I'm aware of. It's possible that other proceedings are under way as well, but I have specific information about this particular case, not about others, unfortunately. For already four years now I've been working outside the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say I've been in a completely different line of work. Of course, I believe that it is simple to receive such information within the next few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As regards action taken by the police or authorised officials, as the appropriate legislation says, you explained during the first part of your testimony that authorised officials act in accordance with the law and without -- even without orders when they establish that a crime had been committed somewhere.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the case in Kosovo and Metohija as well in terms of police conduct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All authorised officials, regardless of where they are within the territory, are duty-bound to act in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the police, are there control mechanisms for monitoring the legality of police activity?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it pertain to internal control only as far as measures taken by policemen are concerned?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only internal control, but it is not final. That is not the last word as far as control is concerned. There is judiciary control over the police and, ultimately, civilian control over the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Tell me quite specifically what was done in order to prevent unlawful action.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of preventing unlawful action in policework, I've already spoken about this up to a certain degree. Many measures were taken, and at every meeting what was highlighted was respect for the constitution and laws of the country and respect for international standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know yourself what the response was to certain unlawful acts committed by policemen?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The response was identical to that in all other cases of commission of crimes. We partly explained the previous table, and we saw there that specifically during the war a total of 12 criminal reports were filed against policemen involving particular cases that resulted in loss of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, what was the attitude of the top echelons of the police in Kosovo and Metohija, the people with top responsibility in terms of legality of police action?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of the top echelons of the police in Kosovo and in Belgrade regarding this question, legality of police activity, was of preeminent importance. I personally saw that this question was given appropriate attention at every meeting and was on the agenda of every meeting. I myself often went there in order to carry out certain tasks upon instructions from my minister. I never failed to convey what the state leadership and police leadership had to say, that in spite of the very difficult conditions involved, the constitution and law had to be observed, as well as international law. I can say that what was dominant in these positions were two particular points that we conveyed to our subordinates, and they came from the position of the top echelons of the ministry, and had to do with the following: That the police in Kosovo and Metohija has to strictly distinguish between terrorists and criminals and other persons who are citizens of the state. The second fact is the fact that we are victims of terrorism and NATO aggression should not lead us astray into crime or anything else that is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in the past few moments, as you explained how the leadership police behaved in Kosovo and Metohija, including leaders of police units, commanders, and other police officials, could you now describe the approach of regular policemen to their work in Kosovo and Metohija and towards legality.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always inspected units, when I had orders to do so, and I always used the opportunity to talk to individual policemen who were involved in specific assignments. It was quite clear that all of them, apart from certain exceptions that I always mention, unless I forget, went to Kosovo and Metohija in the deep conviction that they were defending their country from terrorism, and they understood that as their professional duty and responsibility. And apart from the exceptions which we mentioned on several occasions, all of them were committed to the maximum to respecting all the relevant regulations and legislation governing policework, especially in those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude, however, that despite all the measures taken, there were crimes committed, and is it your testimony that whenever the police found out about such things, they always took legal steps against perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always, regardless of which category the perpetrators belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean whether it was a civilian or a policeman or a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a limit to the number of times the same general proposition can be advanced in slightly different language, that the police always took appropriate action. What I would like to see are examples of that, and they seem to be distinctly lacking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Your Honour, is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a comment on the way in which the same thing is being asked repeatedly without any specification at all emerging from the answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just answering questions, and I really have no other way of answering the questions I'm Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I will now ask you some questions related to the events that are charged in this indictment and that involve loss of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The exhibit -- or tab 76 that may or may not become an exhibit, it's another example, I think, of a document, if we look at it, that is not authored. We know almost nothing about the circumstances of its preparation. We can see that it's marked in the top right-hand corner A2 as if it's an annexure to some other document, but we don't know what document. Now -- and we know from the questions from the Bench and the answers to those questions that no other supporting detail is presently available to us. While I have no desire to burden the Court or myself with additional material, given the time that's going to pass between the conclusion of today's sitting and the resumption of sittings next week, it is open to the accused, alerted as he has been by my observations and by observations from the Court, to provide between now and then material that will give more substance to what these schedules are about. And I should make it clear that I'm reserving my position to object to the production of any of this kind of material on the grounds of its unreliability as thus far evidenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice, and Mr. Milosevic is no doubt grateful for the advice that you have given him. You may wish to follow it, Mr. Milosevic. Ultimately it will be a matter for the Chamber to determine what weight to attach to evidence of this kind. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this question, General, this table in tab 76, is it an official document of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an official document of the Ministry of the Interior, and I am partially familiar with this marking A. The letter A is designate -- designates all cases involving death; murder, et cetera. So whenever you see the mark A, that relates to cases involving death. We have other documents marked by other letters, and they refer to other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, taking into account this last remark made by Mr. Nice, I understand the need to lay the foundation and deal with authenticity, but you have heard testimony here from one chief of secretariat in Kosovo and Metohija, and he dealt with cases and the situation related to one secretariat and its area of responsibility. General Stevanovic is dealing with the entire Kosovo and Metohija. There is a limit to the amount of detail we can go into when dealing with such tables and figures of this type. It would be rational, I believe, for us to present all the underlying documentation that served as a basis for preparing this, but if you believe that is necessary, I can ask that all the documentation supporting these numerical indicators, all the underlying cases, be provided to this Court for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's a matter for you. Proceed to your next subject area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Stevanovic, could you read the title of this tab, tab 76, to us again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title reads: "Overview of security related events involving loss of life that occurred in connection with armed conflicts in Kosovo and Metohija in the period from the 1st of January, 1998, until the 1st of June, 2001, in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, broken down by period -- by time period."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you have any idea why, then, the period from 2nd of June to 31st of December, 2003, is included in the schedule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only because of the fact that incidents involving loss of life continue to be monitored in Kosovo and Metohija to this day, as I mentioned in the answer to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is not mentioned with the title. The title says the period up to 1st of June, 2001, and the schedule expands to the period of 2003. So can I take it somebody edited the schedule at a later time? And who did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not think the table was edited. I believe it is a technical omission. A title from a previous period was used in a new table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, this particular period from the 1 January 1998 to 1 June 2001 ends with a column 7, and then with the passage of time, in all likelihood, the next column was added when updating the date with --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused really mustn't be allowed to start giving evidence, speculating and suggesting things for the witness. If the witness can't answer the question, the accused certainly can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the kind of evidence that would be helpful in relation to this matter that arises under Article 7(3) is evidence that would show a stage-by-stage approach of the authorities in the treatment of an infraction by a soldier or a police officer. The infraction is committed. What is the next step? A report is made. What is the next step? It is sent to the judicial authorities. What is the next step? The Article doesn't actually require punishment. It requires that reasonable measures be taken to punish the perpetrators. So the important thing is to show the application of a judicial procedure to the information that an infraction has been committed. The general's evidence is helpful to a certain degree, but it is at a level of generality, such a level of generality that I think its assistance may be called in question. But it's a matter for you to determine how you present your case. Of course, if you can present the kind of evidence that I have outlined, you should, and I would advise you to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. Robinson. Let me just remind you, however, that during the testimony of General Gojovic, evidence of precisely such a stage-by-stage approach was presented for all cases that were within military jurisdiction. And we can obtain data concerning all these cases involving the police as well, but I have to note that the jurisdiction of the executive government ends at the point when the perpetrator is delivered to the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, maybe I can be of assistance, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am partially familiar with all the documents under these tabs. I haven't had time to read them all since the trial began, but I know that these papers contain at least several cases of the kind that you mentioned, cases wherein a policeman committed a murder and was subjected to the appropriate procedure. I believe we will reach, eventually, such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Utilise the break, and when we return maybe Mr. Milosevic will find it appropriate to lead you to that kind of evidence. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I just wish to draw the witness's attention to the fact that he may use the documents under various tabs. They are located on his right side. And just as everybody else is able to look up potential exhibits, the same possibility is also open to the witness. And I will ask the witness, because I have not had any contact with him since the beginning of his testimony, to find, if he can, specific documents during the break so that we can look at them together. I will now come back to the question that I just asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion, General, to read this indictment?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the police have any knowledge about incidents involving loss of life; in other words, about all these murders and killings cited in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the publication of the indictment, the police was aware only of some incidents involving loss of life that are covered by this indictment. Specifically, the police was aware of the incident in Racak, the incident in Izbica, the incident in Kotlina. It had some information about some of the events in Suva Reka. I cannot remember any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have information about Dubrava, for instance?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dubrava too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now tell us, please, if these other incidents, apart from those that you said the police had information about before the indictment, if these other incidents were not included in official police records, what can that mean?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can only mean that until its withdrawal from Kosovo and Metohija, the police had no information about them whatsoever, including such information as is available from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you think would have been the likely course of action by the police had it had information about such events?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the police would have acted in the same way in which it proceeded with regard to these other events that it was aware of and generally with regard to all the other events involving loss of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could the police react to the incidents that are covered by the indictment?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that yesterday. Until the beginning of the war, the police took appropriate action in at least 1.500 cases involving loss of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, does that mean that if action was taken in 1.500 cases involving loss of life that are not covered by this indictment, would there have been any reason for the police to fail to take action in other cases that are included in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No other reason apart from the fact that we were not aware of them. We had no information, no reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So regarding these events that are not cited and regarding police action in those cases, I will ask you some questions later. Now I would like to ask you something about the incidents cited in the indictment that you were aware of. We will follow the sequence. That is, let's begin with the incident in Racak. General, let's be specific. I'm not going to ask you questions about your knowledge of that event, the event in Racak, but we'll move on straight away to the documents that have to do with Racak and that have been tabled as exhibits here along with your testimony. So in respect of Racak, in the exhibits we have -- actually, the exhibits are to be found in tabs 240 to 262.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give us the number, the binder number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are binders 7, 8, and 9. From 260 until 402. Tabs 260 to 402. I apologise. It was 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we're all ready now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, have you found the exhibits that relate to Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are rather lengthy and to be found in two binders next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what binder it begins with, and tab.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It begins with tab 260 and ends inclusively with tab 402.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Binder 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, looking at this binder, in tab 275, for instance, we have a list from the on-site investigation. Could you tell us what documents 260 to 275 inclusive include with the list of the on-site investigation. What do all these documents refer to, 260 to 275?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these tables, and you can see the contents of the binder at the beginning, you have the criminal reports for the crimes of terrorism which were filed, if I remember, before the event in Racak took place against unknown perpetrators and specific known perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, is there any translation for any of these tabs? If there isn't any, why is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assumed that the translations did exist, because all the documents were given over for translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there any translation? I'm asking the court deputy or the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like to find out if these documents were presented to the Translation Unit for translation. I'd like to find out, if they were presented to the CLSS for translation, when were they presented? Because we cannot continue in this manner with untranslated documents. I understand, Mr. Milosevic, they were presented last Friday. That is not sufficient lead time, as you well know. That's barely a week ago. How do you expect CLSS, even with the favourable treatment which I understand you receive from them, to complete the translation within the period of a week?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not what I expect, Mr. Robinson, but judging by what I know, my information, these documents were sent in far earlier, which means that the documents were submitted for translation, if what you say is true, when General Stevanovic almost started his testimony. There is not a single document which was not sent in for translation since General Stevanovic has been here, and he's been here for quite some time now, so it must have all been before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to consult with my colleagues, because this practice makes the work exceedingly difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, just before we deal with this matter any further, perhaps you could clarify one thing for me. Racak involved MUP officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in the region of 40 or more Albanians were killed. Is there in existence a MUP report about what happened, or are there reports by MUP officers about what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I was not in Kosovo and Metohija, and I was informed about the whole event from daily reports, one of those daily reports being the one we saw yesterday. I can't say at this point whether there are any concrete reports by MUP officers about the event itself. Possibly some documents are to be found in this very long file and binder, but since the very beginning of the event, the entire case was dealt with by the legal organs, the judiciary, and we have documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Answer me then this very simple question, because I thought you were familiar with the documents, but it would appear that you're now going to be asked to engage in a fishing exercise through the documents, but answer me this question: Who was the MUP officer in charge of the MUP contingent at Racak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, it was Goran Radosavljevic who at that time was the assistant head of the staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In view of the discrepancy in information we have received as to when these documents were submitted to the CLSS for translation, I'm going to take a break of five minutes, and the court deputy will inquire from CLSS when the documents were submitted for translation as we cannot continue to operate on the basis of a practice that makes a nonsense of the procedural requirements that are designed to facilitate the smooth running of the Court's proceedings. So the court deputy is to find out when they were submitted and who submitted them. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. We will take a break for five minutes. --- Break taken at 10.07 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The court deputy has been working very hard to try to provide the information that I sought. The matter is fairly complicated. She has not yet concluded her investigations. What we'll do, Mr. Milosevic, is to allow you to lead evidence on some of the tabs which you consider to be very important to your case. So we'll allow you to lead evidence on those tabs that you consider important. We'll have them placed on the ELMO since they're not translated. When the Court deputy's investigations are concluded, the Chamber will announce the position that it will take.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, may I give an explanation which I think would be useful with respect to the problem that has arisen and that we're faced with as far as translations are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just very briefly. It is not the fault of my associates, neither is it the fault of the translation service. It is a question of having an unrealistically brief period of time for the witness's documents, and all the documents have been here for more than a month. There is just too much material. And Professor Rakic has told me that the translation service could not take in more than its quota of 1.000 pages per month, and that was the situation when they were translating the documents for Witness Paponjak. So it's not that they don't wish to accept more material nor that the documents are not at their disposal but they don't have the capacity to follow the dynamics of the testimony with the enormous amount of material. For example, for Momir Bulatovic, the Witness that I have been moving forward constantly precisely because the exhibits haven't been translated yet, although they were all sent in last year -- well, last year, December, if truth be told. But anyway, I have extended that deadline for the witness because the translation service had to deal with the documents for witnesses coming before him. So that this is time constraint, and the translation service just cannot get through the enormous amount of material and provide us with the exhibits we need. When I have all the exhibits, it is of course in my interest to have them all translated as soon as possible and handed over to the translation service. So their capacity is as it stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Let us proceed now. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few general points before we go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in tab 260, according to the description, are they all the documents that the Ministry of the Interior possesses, of the Republic of Serbia, with respect to the event in Racak? Are they all there? And documents which were later on put into the subsequent tabs, 261 to -- onwards?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Tab 261 -- 260 is a list of all the documents that exist and that were later classified in the different tabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do these include criminal reports with respect to terrorist activities? That is the first chapter of the documents. And then the second chapter deals with investigation, the investigation carried out; and the third chapter, KLA documents relevant to Racak; and the fourth chapter the information and intelligence gathered and the law on criminal proceedings. There are many of those documents. Chapter 5 are documents which relate to operative information.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all that is contained in tab 260. Chapter 6 deals with analyses.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Analysis of security related events. And 7, reports, including forensic reports, court reports, various statements with respect to Racak, and all the other documents.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are these all official documents, then, of the Ministry of the Interior, the court organs, and the crime technicians' reports and services? We have a set of photographs, lists with all the investigation that went on. I don't have to enumerate all that now.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is just one case that was entered into the statistical review and overview we looked at earlier on. It has the number -- each document has a number with the A. I have explained what the A refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, for our requirements here, I'm going to use -- or, rather, ask for Mr. Robinson's indulgence, and with his help I should like to ask that a document be placed on the overhead projector. Let me just get the document out. It is tab 400. Could you find tab 400, please. I assume that it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Binder 9.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- readily readable. No, tab 400. Tab 400. I don't know how you came by binder 9. Oh, yes, binder 9. That's right, you're quite right. Binder 9, tab 400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. It's on the ELMO. Let us hear about the provenance first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this a press release of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it issued on the 15th of January, 1999, that is to say on the day when what happened happened in Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, let us see what it says now, this press release. I'll read it out. It's very short. "On the 15th of January, 1999 -" that is to say the same day when the press release is being issued- "the police took measures of blocking the village of Racak, municipality of Stimlje, with a view to finding and arresting members of a terrorist group which on the 10th of January, 1999, carried out a terrorist attack near the village of Slivovo, and in this attack Svetislav Przic, a policeman of the police station in Stimlje, lost his life. The members of this terrorist group carried out several terrorist attacks in the area of Urosevac, and they involved the killing of seven members of the Albanian national minority. The Kosovo Verification Mission of the OSCE was informed about the measures taken." General, even when the consequences were not known as yet, the ministry issued a press release stating that they had blocked the village in order to isolate the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are giving the evidence there. You're giving the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I'm going to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point's destroyed by the way in which you put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I make this point: In a sense it builds on a question by His Honour Judge Bonomy, a question that reflects our own interest, where's the original material? Where's the original report on any event. To produce a press release from a party that may be an interested party is really to produce a self-serving statement. What we're always looking for, especially if material to be provided in this method is going to be limited, is the best source material, and may I simply make this observation at this stage to assist the accused who seems to be having difficulties now conducting his Defence and might, in our respectful submission, be well advised to turn to Mr. Kay for guidance. This -- this material, or some of this material may well be material we've been trying to get from the authorities under requests for assistance that has been denied us over the years. And if this material contains raw material or contemporaneous raw material, it's really to that material that any advocate presenting this part of the accused's case would be concentrating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it were favourable to his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, if it were favourable to his case one would expect that to be the first document to which an advocate would turn, not a press release, which is always capable or subject to criticism and scepticism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no intention to lead. This is a self-explanatory document. Mr. Robinson, it is dated the 15th of January. That's when what happened happened in Racak. That is an indisputable fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What it doesn't say is that "We are issuing this document before we know the full consequences of what happened at Racak," and your question was, "Does this prove that the government announced this before the full consequences were known?" That's where the leading element came into the question. It was about matters which are not actually in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, please help us clarify something. Was it known that in the area of Racak there was a KLA group that had carried out a series of killings in that town?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were any measures taken because of that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of measures?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, police action was taken to find and arrest members of the group, the terrorist group that was in the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This police action in terms of finding the terrorist group that was in the village of Racak, was the Verification Mission of the OSCE informed about that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how come a clash occurred in the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from the information that I received while I was in Belgrade and I know it from the materials that I later on read about that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more specifically how this clash occurred in the village of Racak on the basis of the information that you had and the events that occurred on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would invite the Chamber first to require from this witness identification of the sources of information and production of them if they're in written form. We've been going around the issue of -- in the Defence case, the issue of Racak without ever descending to a particular document that sets out the history as perceived or asserted by the MUP. His Honour's question drew the answer about Goran Radosavljevic, and the Chamber will remember that indeed we've seen Goran Radosavljevic in a clip from The Fall of Milosevic explaining what he did, a clip that wasn't admitted into evidence although the whole transcript of the interview that that man had with the OTP has been provided to the accused, and that's about as near as we've got, I think, to raw material constituting an account, apart from the reports that are maybe partial and selective that were put in through Marinkovic. And I might as well tell the Chamber, because there's no point -- there's no advantage to me in keeping this from you, and I don't seek advantage, we are engaged in a process, because we think it will help the Chamber, of trying to find all the Serb side contemporary sources, and there may be further ones in these untranslated documents, that will eventually assist you if the accused doesn't do it himself. But this question, in our respectful submission, which may be pointed at the same general topic, should only be allowed to be answered if he can identify his sources and produce those in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I certainly agree with the first part. General, tell us the sources of the information that you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I was assistant minister of the interior, which is a known fact, and I was in Belgrade. Every major operation that was carried out by the police in Kosovo and Metohija and every important event that happened in Kosovo, regardless of the police, was the subject of daily urgent reports received by the minister and the assistant ministers. On the very same day I knew that this action was being planned and carried out, and the same day I was aware of the content of this press release. In addition to that, since the said event assumed the proportions it did, I always tried to follow closely from Belgrade everything that was going on, because this particular event received a great deal of media attention, as you know. I can also assist by saying that towards the end of this binder there are a few documents which clearly indicate what the preceding history of this event is, what specifically happened on that day and what happened during the following days until the case was closed, so to speak. Of course, I can show some other tabs, too, if you think that I'm the one who should do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What are the documents you say are in the folders here, binders here, which say what happened on the 15th of January? You can take us to these, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour. I just need a few seconds to have a look at what I have at hand right now. Tab 394 is called "Analysis of previous security related incidents that caused --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you for documents that record what actually happened on the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 397 is entitled "Report on the chronology of events in the village of Racak." Perhaps it would be best to have a look at that document, because quite a bit can be found in there; what happened beforehand, what happened during the actual operation, and what happened later in respect of the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be placed on the ELMO. Mr. Milosevic, you must be familiar with this document. Let the witness direct his attention to those passages which will show us what happened on the 15th. Tell us first, General, about the document itself; who prepared it, how it was prepared.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is an integral part of the case file that has to do with what happened in Racak. It clearly shows that it has the form of a report as to what preceded the event, what measures were taken during the event itself and in its immediate aftermath. Most probably it was drafted at the MUP staff in Pristina and exceptionally perhaps it could have been done at the MUP secretariat in Urosevac which was the secretariat that was locally in charge of the area. And certainly it constituted an integral part of the appropriate report or the accompanying document through which this was sent to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it not part of the practice in your office to put some indication on very important documents like this of who was responsible for compiling them, just a reference initial or something to locate the person responsible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is customary for this kind of document not to have such elements, but it is usually an integral part of a daily report or an accompanying document, and then it is attached to such a document and sent to an appropriate person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's part of a larger document. Presumably at the end of that larger document there would be the initial or the signature of the person who prepared it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said during my previous answer. I said accompanying document. Probably there was such a document, usually on one page only, very brief, and it would usually say, "Please find enclosed," et cetera, et cetera, and then the title of the document would follow. Of course, I do not see such a piece of paper here in this file, but possibly it was part of the daily reports that we mentioned. Certainly when this event occurred it was included in the daily report that the staff provided the following day to the ministry in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So rather than being at the end, it might have about at the beginning, but you can't actually pinpoint the cover page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I cannot identify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The document is about five or six pages, and there are dates --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- so it does appear to deal with the day in question. The question is how to approach it since it's not translated. It's translated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we certainly have a translation of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're trying to find the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The last document was also translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the 400 was translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We -- I received some translations recently, so I'm checking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To save time, I can make my unmarked copy available now, if that will save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Kwon and I will share that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I find surprising is that you can't tell us what this document actually is. It looks important, and your position, I would have thought you would have known what it actually was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this question is addressed to me, I can answer, Your Honour. Of course I know what this is about. Perhaps it was a slip of the tongue if I said that I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that you say that you know what it's about. What is not clear -- well, what I thought you were in doubt about was what the document actually was; who compiled it, for what purpose, what it was supposed to be, and it's disappointing that you cannot tell us that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only provided an alternative answer. I'm certain that it is a document that was drafted in the secretariat in Pristina or, alternatively, in the secretariat of Urosevac, which was the one that had jurisdiction. I was superior at the level of the ministry. I only visited the area occasionally, and I have difficulty answering questions that deal with the technical level. This is a very voluminous material, compiled by a number of various people, and I am aware of it only in general terms. It would have been different if a specific task group had been appointed to draft this, which I don't believe was the case, but this is the material that was drafted just after the event happened, and we can present it at a later stage. And there was a plan, perhaps, for action to be taken after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do we tell when it was drafted, sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible indeed that the last page is missing here, because we obviously can't see the date on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists, I'm not going to object to the reading of this document at this stage. Its production may be another matter, but for my own reasons there are some parts of it that I have an interest in in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But reading the entire document would take too much time. Mr. Milosevic, can you direct the witness to those areas of the document that would provide information as to -- as to what happened. It's entitled "Chronology of events in the village of Racak."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. Robinson. I was waiting for you to receive answers to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, is it clearly indicated in this document what the aim of police measures in Racak was on the 15th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is indicated already in the first line of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With -- in order to arrest the terrorist group, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And at the end of this passage, what can we read? It says in order to arrest a terrorist group, it follows an explanation of what kind of terrorist group it was, what they had done, and the passage ends with the words?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the morning of 15th January, 1999, the action aimed at arresting the terrorist group in the village of traffic commenced."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it say which unit was engaged to undertake police measures against this group in Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see that in paragraph two at the very beginning of the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to the information contained in these tabs, operative information, Official Notes, et cetera, do we see that police was aware of the numbers, the numerical strength of this terrorist group in this area?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the documents contained in these tabs, we have clear indication and clear information about the numbers involved, but I do not know the exact number of members of this terrorist group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the number that we can find here -- and by the way, during the testimony of Witness Jasovic, we saw documents that indicated that in this area there were between 80 and 120 members of terrorist groups. I know that it can be found in reports pre-dating the 15th. So my question is: In view of the presence of this terrorist group in Racak, would the use of a police company that numbered perhaps 15 [as interpreted] be adequate to the task?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's something I'm not clear about. You were asked whether in view of the presence of this terrorist group would the use of a police company that numbered 15 be adequate, and you said yes. What was the actual size of the -- the group that was assigned to Racak, or have I misunderstood? I think the previous information was that a company of 110 policemen were assigned. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not -- no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. The interpreters apologise. It was the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am receiving the English interpretation and that's interfering, but I cannot hear Serbian in my headphones. Yes, I can hear the B/C/S booth clearly now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not mention 15 men. I mentioned the 15th of January. I didn't follow the transcript, though. I was just asking, would the use of a police company of 110 men be adequate from the police point of view to the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for the clarification, because the transcript referred to a police company that numbered 15 as being adequate, which was why I raised the question. That was the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an error, because 15 is less than a squad. It certainly couldn't be a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We see a reference here, General, in paragraph number three of this document, to the notorious Sadik Mujota. Do we see why he was notorious?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can clearly understand that from the text below. He had committed several murders of policemen, and he had kidnapped a large number of citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do we see from the document when this operation began?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see that from the next paragraph. It says it started at 0300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we see when fire was opened and who opened it first?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see that in the next paragraph, which says that fire was opened when the police were advancing towards the village of Racak from the direction of Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who opened fire?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terrorists, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, did you have occasion to listen to the testimony of the commander of that zone of the KLA, Mr. Shukri Buja, when he testified here?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did, but not in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention, Mr. Robinson, that Witness Shukri Buja, who testified here for the side of Mr. Nice, confirmed in cross-examination that they had opened fire from a heavy machine-gun at the police as the police was coming into Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that fire was returned. Do we have a description here of all the weapons from which fire was opened at the police as they were coming into Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the same paragraph, that is the last paragraph on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph I would like to draw your attention to what is written on the first page.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is written there? Does it say: "Strong fire was opened at police force members from heavy -- from mortars, hand-held rocket launchers --"

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Browning 12.7-millimetre light machine-guns and infantry weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is at the very end. One policeman was transferred to the clinical hospital centre in Pristina. Is that written there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the last paragraph at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it say how the police entering Racak were armed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph two on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the police use any heavy weapons in Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see from this text that the heaviest weapon was a machine-gun of 62-millimetre calibre, and we see from the previous paragraph that they had anti-aircraft machine-guns and other higher calibre weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in view of all these facts, can we speak about any disproportionate force used against the terrorists in Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the weapons used on both sides, we can certainly not talk about any disproportionate force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, by the way, the accused has for the second time in the course of these proceedings characterised the evidence of Shukri Buja in a certain way. I'm not sure that it's an accurate characterisation. The evidence can be found on pages 6313 and thereabouts and, the Chamber may recall, speaks of first shots being by way of warning shots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But coming from who?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From the KLA side but as warning shots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the questions I asked very well. I asked at whom those shots were fired, and Shukri Buja answered at the Serbian police, and I'm sure it can be found in the transcript. What could warning shots mean if they are fired at somebody? I really can't understand. If you are firing at somebody, that means you're firing to kill, not to be -- not to warn the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us avoid the comments at this stage. Move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, what do you find especially typical and characteristic in all this, to cut the long story short?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph on the second page, we can see the stage-by-stage progression in the use of weapons, including calls to the terrorists to surrender. The terrorists refused to surrender while at the same time retreating towards the villages of Luznica and Petrovo in Stimlje municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just direct us to the passage. Oh, I see it now, yes. "Despite appeals to surrender," yes. Yes, continue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly in the next paragraph we see that 40 terrorists were liquidated, most of whom were wearing the uniforms of the so-called KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, tell us if we can read in this paragraph which you quoted from that the police was shot at from trenches, bunkers, and communicating trenches prepared in advance?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you indeed establish later that that was indeed so, that there were bunkers, trenches and communicating trenches, including this heavy machine-gun nest?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could establish that although I was not on the spot myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything else here that you believe to be particularly characteristic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next paragraph speaks about the quantities of weapons found, and after that paragraph there is a passage dealing with the work of the team preparing for an on-site investigation and all the following action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us now turn to the very end of the document, where it says at the -- in the middle of the page: "Based on the description of actions taken by the police earlier, one can conclude --" and so on and so forth, and then it says in the penultimate line: "During the use of firearms, the police force did not overstep their authority. The police intervened and used firearms --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. The usher has not yet placed it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. General, would you please read these last couple of lines or perhaps something else that you deem necessary, but certainly those lines at the end that I started quoting.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last three lines of the concluding part of this document read: "In their use of firearms -- in the use --" "During their official action, the police was constantly under strong fire from various weapons, various heavy weapons, from various facilities, and they were forced to use weapons themselves." Penultimate line: "In their use of firearms, the police force did not overstep their authority." The last line: "The police intervened and used firearms in accordance with the law, gradually, selectively and correctly." This seems to be the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, in view of the fact that it all seems to have happened fairly early in the morning, with the consequences which you've just outlined, why do you think the press release made no reference at all to the deaths of terrorists, even in a vague way, but recorded the death of the police officer who died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point, I cannot say when the statement, the press statement was compiled. Possibly it was drafted in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the early hours of the morning, when people went to work. The police usually in its first statements does not give out any specific information, like the number of victims and similar information and data, until they are reliably established, because specific figures or concrete data can give rise to unrest among the public, particularly if they are proved to be incorrect later on. It is only on the basis of a subsequent investigation that one would be able to see the exact number of casualties, their structure and so on. That is, of course, my opinion based on my experience when press communiques of this kind are drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, now, with respect to what Mr. Bonomy just asked you, in what sense in this statement for the public of the 15th of January is the death of the policeman mentioned?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the death of the policeman --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Don't assume, please, but take a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I take a look at the document I'll be able to tell you. The death of the policeman is mentioned here, of a policeman, and the event took place on the 10th of January, and the death of the policeman was one of the reasons for the action. The death of the policeman was not mentioned during the operation itself, but it is mentioned as a cause or pretext for the action to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether when the police entered Racak there were any OSCE verifiers there for them to be able to see what happened in Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know full well that they had been informed, and I saw on some footage or a picture the presence of their vehicles immediately after the operation and during it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned several documents which you considered to be important. I really do not have a list of what -- which of those have been translated and which haven't. Could you just point out the most important documents to us now, please, because you spoke of the chronology of events and indicated the plan of action in similar situations and the important documents in these files, in these binders. So which documents did you have in mind? Which documents would you like to focus on?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, tab 396 is a document which relates to throwing light on the circumstances under which the crime of terrorism was committed, dated the 10th of January, and referred to in this statement in which a policeman was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not only an elucidation of the circumstances referring to the act of terrorism on the 10th of January but the 15th of January, 1999, in the village of Racak as well. That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that is linked with the intervention. So here we have an explanation of the cause, and then in the second paragraph they go on to describing the event in similar terms as we found in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read out the second paragraph of the document that you have before you now.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second paragraph reads as follows: "On the 15th of January, 1999, in the early hours of the morning, with the intention of apprehending a terrorist group who had killed policemen Svetislav Przic, they blocked the village of Racak, Stimlje municipality, the approach roads to the terrorist groups from fortifications, trenches and so on, attacked the police using automatic rifles, mortars, et cetera, at the approaches to the village. On the occasion the policeman Goran Vucicevic was wounded and a number of MUP vehicles damaged. The police responded to the gunfire and broke up the terrorist group on that occasion. A number of terrorists were killed." And then it lists the weapons that were confiscated on the occasion, and of course after that we have information about the investigation. On paragraph two, page 2, it is clearly stated that the beginning of the drive to apprehend the terrorists, the Kosovo Verification OSCE Mission was informed, which was present on location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the footage that we saw by Reuters, we saw the police entering the village and two jeeps on the hill above Racak, orange in colour, that belonged to the Verification Mission. General, do you consider that it would be important to indicate another document to us? We don't have the translations, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to single out tab 395 as well. It is a plan for the implementation of operational and tactical measures and investigative operations with respect to identifying the terrorist group, its members and activities in the area of Racak village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it say here "Plan for the implementation of operational and tactical measures -" and the number is 52, the 20th of January, 1999, is the date, is that right - "with respect to throwing light on the act of terrorism..."?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise what you're reading out. I see. You mean the title page. Yes, the title page. It says "Plan for the implementation of operational and tactical measures and investigative operations -" the number is 52, dated the 20th of January, 1999 - "with respect to throwing light on the circumstances under which the act of terrorism was committed on the 10th of January," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand you. Do you mean the tab or the origins of the document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the origins of the document, this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately I have to repeat myself and say that this document is in the official MUP files. What we have is a copy of that official document stored in the MUP. And in the upper left-hand corner they have A/6-025. That is the number at the top there, on the left. And perhaps this is a good occasion for me to repeat and explain what I've already said with respect to the document analysed. So the title page -- without the title page it would be difficult for us to recognise and establish what number the document is recorded under and the date, and I had a problem there. But if you look at the title page, then you'll see that the document does indeed have a date and a number to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, let's explain what the plan is about. It says: "Plan for the implementation of operational and tactical measures and investigative operations."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, General, it would be very useful to us all if you were to explain to us what the operational and tactical measures were and the investigation conducted because it is the plan to implement those measures; operational, tactical, investigative, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the answer comes, unless others' documents are different from mine, we don't have the cover page in translation which exists in Serbian, and one can see from the cover page in Serbian that the -- there are two parts to the document, the attachment or whatever they are. One is the plan and the second one is a document we don't seem to have. So that the title page may be of some significance, and the other document may need to be identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is your copy of the plan preceded by a letter dated the 20th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In English, no, I just have the plan. I have the plan like this. It starts with the heading "Plan."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two pages after that I have a letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm surprised. You don't have the translation of Plan, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, we don't. I just have three pages starting -- headed "Plan," but that's clearly not the complete Serbian document which is preceded by a cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have that plus a letter which obviously accompanied the plan, dated the 20th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
