utterances.text: Is there a reason why Judge Kwon and myself have not been provided with translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the document His Honour Judge Bonomy has doesn't accord with the original either, because the page that I'm missing from the original is not a letter, it's a short document that has a handwritten part to it identifying two probable annexures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As you're in a mood to assist, Mr. Nice, you might let us have that copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what I'm missing in translation. And that identifies, as I hold it up, the two parts of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can see that in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But we don't have that in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What has been written in in hand here says "Plan," and after that it says "Elucidation." But in this tab, apart from the handwritten word "Plan," I don't see the next part, the elucidation of circumstances. So I assume that the document contains both the plan and how light was thrown on the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This cover page obviously contains two documents. If you take a look at it, the first document is within tab 395 itself. The second document, relating to the elucidation of the circumstances, is tab 396.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Fine. We seem to have cleared that point up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, it's being copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This plan, General, of implementing operational and tactical measures, as far as I can see, contains several groups of tasks and assignments.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The first group of tasks, under 1, identifying the terrorist group, its members and activities in the area of Racak village; is that right? Is that what it is?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite obviously this plan is composed of two parts. The first is I, which relates to operational and tactical measures taken by the police force; and II --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just see Arabic numerals. I don't see Roman numerals.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Roman numeral is just above the Arabic number, to the left. We have I and then 1, and then page 2 is II, and it relates -- as I said, I relates to tactical measures taken by the police and operational ones, II steps taken in which the police cooperates with the pertinent organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to I. What do those measures contain? It says here: "1. Identifying the terrorist group, its members and activities," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. So the first task is to identify the terrorist group as well as its measures and its members and its activities in the area of the village of Racak. And then there is a further breakdown. A is the group's organisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. We will not proceed until -- we will not proceed until Judge Kwon and I have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to note that they don't have the translation either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let the interpreters also have translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, did you hear what I said? I said we'll not proceed until Judge Kwon and I have received translations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did hear you. I heard you very well, but I understood that you had received a copy in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we haven't. What page are you -- what page are you on now, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May we just look at the structure of the document. It is divided into three parts, denoted with Roman numerals.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe even four, four parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes, four parts. Now, with respect to the steps and measures undertaken, I, identifying the terrorist group, its members and activities in the area of Racak village.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And those are classical police operational and tactical measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just go through the different chapters. Let's go on to II and then you'll be able to explain to us. Part II: "Acting on orders from the investigating judge in the district court of Pristina," and then pursuant to orders by the public prosecutor, district public prosecutor. So then we have the police, then the investigating judge, then the district public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The whole thing is the police, but in the first part the police acts independently and then, secondly, pursuant to orders from the investigating judge, and in part III pursuant to orders from the district public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have the translation and we can go ahead and see what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, what was planned, under Arabic 1, is "Identifying the terrorist group, its members and activities in the area of Racak village," and then that is divided into theses, that is to say, how those tasks are to be realised, and the people in charge of realising that task are listed. We see that the implementers, that is A and B, are the MUP staff in Pristina, Urosevac, and in Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the local centres.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have the centre in Gnjilane and the SUP centre in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is about the organisation of the group. A is the group's organisation, and B are the material established facts?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Later on, we see that we have crime identification and the corpses of the terrorist group, identification of the members of the groups based on the photographs found on site, and the establishment of previous terrorist acts by looking -- of the terrorists by looking at the case files, so on. And under B it is the staff in Pristina and the crime investigation department. So the implementers are the same under V -- under C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does the OE mean; operative evidence? Operative evidence of the state security; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then the other records that are kept, the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Part of these documents, the documents which were established later on and checked out later on, are they on the list of documents that you quoted in tab 260 which provides a list of all the documents that relate to Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That tab, or the first group of documents do contain excerpts of concrete documents from the state security department and the crime files and records relating to public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because I want to link up what we see here when it says documents provided in the files, and you said that the list is to be found in tab 260; is that right? The list provided according to go the groups as we quoted them.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And this plan quite obviously was the basis or one of the bases for the compiling of the entire file or dossier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, haven't we had enough of this -- this plan?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was my understanding that the witness had a few more things to say in relation to this document, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those that he considered to be of significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So far as your case is concerned, why do we need anything more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, what is the relevance of this to the case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume, Mr. Bonomy, that it's relevant to see how the police, in accordance with regulations and their duties, acted in this particular case. When all of this is cross-referenced with the data that you have in these binders, then it is quite clear that this is a clash between the police and a terrorist group in the area of Racak and the inaccurate assertions made in that paragraph - you know which one it is - where it says that the police committed some killings there. Those were no murders. These were persons who got killed in a clash between a terrorist group and the police. And you will allow that that is quite different from murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, I take it that nobody in the MUP thought that it might be worth investigating the activities of the police on this occasion? Nobody found it odd that there was nobody killed on the Serb side and 40 people killed, perhaps more, on the other side, that there were no prisoners apparently taken? No one thought, in the MUP, that that might merit at least a cursory independent investigation, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the document that we analysed a few moments ago, elements can be seen that show how the police acted on that day according to this chronology of events. These facts lead to the conclusion that the police really acted there the way they would have acted in any similar case. That is to say that it had been established that fire had not been opened before the police unit was attacked, and all the other facts that I don't wish to repeat now because they're all contained in the document we quoted from a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, at the end of the document, in tab 397, there is a sentence that we quoted. "The members of the police did not overstep their duties." Does that mean that before this kind of thing is stated an investigation had to be carried out in order to see whether authority had been overstepped?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what this conclusion should be based on. And in the preceding text they were explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it says: "The police intervened and used firearms in accordance with the law, gradually, selectively and correctly." So in response to Mr. Bonomy's question, did it -- did anybody want to have this checked? Doesn't it emanate from here that it was checked and that this was the conclusion reached?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what stems from that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, after that pointless leading question, let me make it clear that I would be interested to see how that investigation was carried out. It's that investigation, not the investigation into the terrorist activity after the event, that seems to me to be most relevant to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in order to have something like this written in a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you understand the point being made by Judge Bonomy? It's one thing to cite, as you have done --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I haven't finished. It's one thing to cite, as you have done, a statement showing the result of an investigation and which exonerates the police, but that may be seen as self-serving, and that is why it is important to get information about the actual investigation. These statements may be dismissed as being self-serving.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you can discard whatever you wish, but I assume -- I am, rather, putting a very specific question to General Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can this kind of statement be inserted in a document without previously establishing whether it is correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be inserted otherwise. It is the result of measures taken in order to establish these facts. Of course, in the preceding section some of these most relevant facts are referred to. The investigation probably involves a series of notes as to who said what, but obviously it's not contained in here. However, the result of this kind of investigation is this assessment, and it is in accordance with the regulations on the use of force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, we don't even know who made the assessment, never mind have some of the material that indicates how the investigation was conducted. Do you understand our anxiety to see what actually went on following this event to investigate it? And it's as if the Defence is conducted to dance around the issue and avoid engaging on the issue that the Court really wants to hear about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, could you help me: What important issue this is that I've been dancing around?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How the conduct of the police was independently investigated following Racak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I could have taken part in -- or, rather, had I been able to take part in preparing these documents, I would have been in a position to give an answer to that question of yours. I would have asked for individual statements about interviews conducted with individuals, and I probably would have brought them here. I personally think that this report should be trusted. Of course when the police completes a particular action, these documents show that then the judiciary organs become involved, and the police investigation itself cannot affect the judicial investigation, the investigation carried out by the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, with all due respect to you, that's a smokescreen because you know perfectly well there was no judicial investigation of the conduct of the police on this occasion. So please concentrate on what matters here. You've heard the Prosecutor already say today that they've been trying for years to get their hands on the material that relates to this and are grateful to see some of it now percolating through. You're in the ministry. You must have some knowledge of why it has been so difficult to get to the material that will tell us the answer to these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, please bear in mind what I showed you here, that is to say, a certificate related to a request put in by my associates, that after I submitted this request it took 14 months for me to obtain the documents that I asked for, and that is what is contained in that certificate, because there wasn't the least bit of a wish to make available to be me documents that would be helpful to me. So all of 14 months had to go by before we received this documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, do you know whether a court investigation was carried out in relation to what happened in Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that forensic expertise was carried out as well?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether during the court investigation or during the forensics expertise it could have been concluded that there was any kind of execution involved?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Professor Dobricanin, who testified here as a forensic expert in view of the bullet direction, fully rejected the possibility that death was due to execution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you know better than that. You know better than that. "Are you aware that so-and-so fully rejected..." Really, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, when you say that you're aware there was a court investigation, are you saying there was a court investigation into the conduct of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wish to say that there was a court investigation in relation to the actual event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My concern about the previous question was that a question suggesting that Professor Dobricanin testified as a forensic expert doesn't fit with my recollection of the circumstances in which he gave evidence and is clearly aimed at extracting answers from the witness built on the confidence he may feel at that incorrect summary of the position evidentially of Dobricanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. He testified as a fact witness, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct, Mr. Robinson, that Professor Dobricanin testified as a fact witness here. However, during the cross-examination, he gave very precise answers to Mr. Nice's questions that had to do with the presentation of facts that were later established as to where the casings were, as to where the bullets were, and he answered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Nice's point is correct that you misrepresented his status in testifying here. Now, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Robinson, I assume that what is written should be beyond any reasonable doubt, so I'm going to ask the general about 66(a) as it is worded in relation to Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in view of all the facts you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic. Let us find 66(a). And bear in mind you can't ask him to answer the question which is ultimately for the Chamber to decide. You may, however, ask him about particular aspects, but you can't ask him to answer the question which it is our duty to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just going to ask the general to answer questions that he can answer on the basis of the reports he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here in paragraph 66(a), General, it says: "On or about the 15th of January, 1999, in the early morning hours, the village of Racak was attacked by forces of the FRY and Serbia. After shelling, the forces of the FRY and Serbia entered the building later --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The village, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- later in the morning and began conducting house-to-house searches. Villagers who attempted to flee from the forces of the FRY and Serbia were shot throughout the village. A group of approximately 25 men attempted to hide in a building but were discovered by the forces of FRY and Serbia. They were beaten and then were removed to a nearby hill where they were shot and killed. Altogether, the forces of the FRY and Serbia killed approximately 45 Kosovo Albanians in and around Racak." I'm asking you, on the basis of all the facts and all the knowledge that you have, whether this is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a pointless question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is exactly what I said you could not ask. You may ask him about particular aspects of the allegations. There are several aspects to that allegation in 66(a). As to whether the allegation is true or not is a matter for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would respectfully say that the witness can't answer questions about this allegation, even broken into parts, because he wasn't there, he wasn't a witness, he hasn't even been the analyst of materials. He can only and should only deal with matters that are within his knowledge, and he can't express any opinion, in our submission, on the substantive allegations made in 66(a). While I'm on my feet, can I repeat an observation for the Chamber to consider perhaps at later stage. Does not the presentation of this part of his case by the accused, if it is in the way it is because he doesn't understand the procedure and cannot deal with the procedure, show the need for more intervention of the assigned counsel with witnesses of this complexity? I invite the Chamber to consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. As to the first point you raised, we do take in hearsay here. It may not be of much value. But, Mr. Milosevic, you need to bear that in mind. The witness can only provide an answer to questions relating to specific areas on the basis of information that he received. We have had evidence from witnesses who are much closer to this event, and very little will be gained by you by getting second and third and fourth-rate hearsay on this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson. I will reduce this to only a couple of questions. However, in view of what Mr. Nice said that Mr. Obradovic was not even -- Mr. Stevanovic was not even an analyst of the information --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- I have to ask you, Witness, whether you analysed the information and reports that you received?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have reviewed most of the documents in these binders. I cannot remember them by heart, each and every one, because it is a very voluminous file, but I was informed immediately after the event in Racak of the course of events. And coming back to one of your previous questions, I want to add that I personally called Mr. Dobricanin on one occasion when the reports by Mrs. Helena Ranta came in, and I asked him, "Doctor, is there any evidence that these people could have been massacred and executed?" And he answered, "Looking at autopsy reports --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: His evidence on that can't improve on the evidence that we got from the professor. There is no point the witness providing that evidence. We have already heard from the professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to certain matters you have covered here analysing previous documents, since the allegation is being made here that FRY and Serbian forces came in the next morning after shelling, I would like to ask you, was any military unit involved in Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of. All the information I have indicates that fire was first opened at the police unit that was advancing towards the village and then fighting ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Looking and quoting from documents that we have reviewed recently, you listed the weapons that were available to the police unit engaged in Racak. Do you remember that? It was about an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This police unit in Racak, did it use any artillery weapons that could be used for shelling?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all my information, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that there was any shelling of Racak prior to the entry of the police forces?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, if what you mean by "shelling" implies artillery or mortar shells. According to all I know, fire was opened against terrorists only from weapons that we listed in one of the previous passages, and the highest calibre of those weapons was 7.62 millimetres on an APC, and that cannot be qualified as shelling even in theory. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 7.62 millimetre from an APC? It seems to be the same calibre as from an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same calibre but it is a different profile of the rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no shelling?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to all your information, there was no shelling?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone report to you or did you get any information that would arouse suspicion about a possible execution?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, apart from maybe media reports, foreign media reports. I saw nothing of the kind in all the official documents from the judiciary or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We saw from one of the previous documents that a police company was involved numbering 110.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that a regular police unit? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a company from the special police units, as I explained previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of such a structure of the police unit involved, would it have been possible for the whole thing to result in any execution of either KLA or civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not allowing that question. It just invites opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic, when you say there was nothing to arouse your suspicion that there had been a massacre other than press reports, are you saying that there was no formal notification of concern from the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of any OSCE official notification addressed to ministries. There may have been such notification to the Ministry of the Interior. All I know are media reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say media reports, do you mean the statement made by William Walker?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's primarily the one I mean, because it was followed by a number of different comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, among these exhibits we have from tabs 260 to 402, 142 documents related to Racak. On the basis of all these documents -- or, rather, in all these documents can we find any grounds for the allegations made in 66(a)?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I based all my answers on the documentation in these binders and all the information I had in view of my official position in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are there documents here that include forensic reports and the results of the paraffin glove tests that were made on the corpses of those found in Racak?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is not a particular subtle attempt to turn this witness into an expert to get him to express an expert opinion on a range of documents without providing us with the courtesy of a report or any other analysis into those documents which, what is it, 140 -- 142 documents. This line of questioning, in my respectful submission, should not be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The last question which he asked was whether there are documents that include forensic reports and the results of the paraffin glove tests. That's a question of fact. He can answer that. If he proceeds any further, we'll attend to that. You can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have knowledge that on the corpses of certain individuals the paraffin glove test came positive, and I know from my profession the meaning of that test, but I did have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in the position you were in in the police force or, rather, in the Ministry of the Interior, or perhaps in the staff of the MUP in Pristina, was there any suspicion present that any policeman might have committed a crime in Racak?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no such suspicions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If there had been such suspicion, would a separate investigation have been conducted on what transpired?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you conduct an investigation in every single case when there was a reasonable suspicion?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I would like to produce these tabs related to Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What tabs are these?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are willing to admit them. From 260 to 402, all of them including documents related to Racak. As the witness confirmed, in each and every case these are official records of the police, forensic reports including photographs, fingerprints, and all kinds of information such as Official Notes, et cetera. Official records of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The short answer is that I'd invite the Court to make no such decision at the moment in any event. I was just looking for binder 7. Yes, I've found it. The short answer is I'd invite you to make no decision at the moment. A slightly longer observation is that it must be unacceptable to try and put in this quantity of detailed material with the cursory and unacceptable method of examination we've seen so far. The next point is more substantial and detailed, the Court may wish to turn its attention to tab -- as an example, to tab 263 -- no, 260 -- yes, 263 will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Binder 7. If the Court has a look at 263 as an example and casts its eyes to the bottom right-hand corner of the document, it will see a couple of familiar names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have a translation? I don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This one doesn't matter because the Court will be familiar with the names at the bottom right-hand corner of 263. There are a very large number of documents bearing these two signatures. This part of the collection, that is the early part, and also much later. We haven't done -- at least, I haven't done a complete check. Certainly so far as the later documents bearing these two names are concerned, they are simply duplications of what's now in the Jasovic binder, and the admissibility of those documents is specifically on hold, and in my submission must remain on hold until that witness comes back for cross-examination, which looks now not likely to be until the week after next. In any event, the admissibility of material like this must be tested against the requirement of reliability of the Court's Rules, and I intend, when I have a chance, which I haven't so far, to review and consider these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is this the same kind of document that is in the Jasovic documents that are on hold?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 263 is, I think, the same kind of document, and for most of the documents bearing the signatures of these two men they are actually identical documents which are to be found in the Jasovic binder. Parenthetically, I observe it's possible that the accused is piling in for translation documents that have already been translated or been presented for translation before. I don't know the answer to that. Although in the same parenthesis I observe that many other documents I think produced in these 17 binders may have been produced earlier in the Marinkovic documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just hearing the legal arguments because we have already decided that the admissibility will be determined at the end of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. So I would ask the Court, for all these documents, to put the position on hold, and I think admissibility of these documents may be a somewhat detailed exercise of consideration later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But may I observe, though, Mr. Nice, that you can't really have it all ways if one of your basic propositions is that if all of this had been submitted and certified by the ministry, then we could have considered it. Now, subject to the problem of timing, which I do understand because of the when it's coming in, what is the real difference between that, apart from a little weight, in the same material being presented by a senior official of the ministry and saying that these are all genuine records of ours?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the documents are relied upon for their truth, then the question of their reliability is a freestanding issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the questions were quite carefully framed. Ultimately when Mr. Milosevic asked the question, "Was there anything in the material you --" or at least, the witness answered it this way: "There is nothing in the material I saw to indicate a reason for investigating the police at Racak." Now, rightly -- that's an answer that we would have to evaluate, but it's not based on a statement, an assertion of the truth of the facts. It's based on, "Well, I've investigated what material there was and there was nothing to indicate that in that material." Now, that is -- seems to me a perfectly legitimate approach to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that in itself -- I'm sorry I shouldn't ask a question. But Your Honour's observation would suggest that answer in itself might permit in 142 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's possibly so, because I don't see the distinction at the moment between that answer letting them in and the certificate from the ministry letting them in, except the only difference being the timing, that if you get them well before the oral hearing, you have a chance to consider them and deal with them, but it may be very difficult to deal with that volume of documents coming at this stage, which is a separate matter, I think, from the authenticity of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points there: When I drew to Your Honour's attention that we required as long ago as 2001 production of these documents and hadn't received an answer from the ministry, receiving some documents at later stages in other -- by other routes, I wasn't saying that merely the production of the documents to us in answer to a request for assistance would make them admissible in Court in anybody's hands. Documents coming to this building in The Hague doesn't mean they automatically go before this Court in an adversarial process, because one side or the other has to justify their admission. The process of admitting a document or having a document admitted as an exhibit is first get it; second, look at it to see how it helps you; and third, then seek to put it in as an exhibit. And simply to have a volume of material here and then to ask a generally negative question: "Have you looked at the entire archives of Serbia and Montenegro?" "Yes, I have." "Is there anything in them that supports the suggestion X in the Racak allegation?" "No, there isn't." And for that to allow the entire archive go in cannot, in my respectful submission, be correct. The documents have to be one by one admissible according to your Rules -- or our Rules. And so I would press the Court to make absolutely no decision at the moment about these documents until it's heard the cross-examination and seen what points may be made about them. Secondly, the difficulties of dealing with the document is a separate issue and one that may well justify exclusion of documents certainly from now on. I have been extremely, I hope, accommodating within the limitations of the resources available to me but I cannot go on being accommodating where there's a risk that important points to assist the Chamber are likely to be missed through the late presentation of material. Now, this material came in, I don't know, ten days ago in part in an untabbed mass. Rather than wait for the tabbed documents, we used resources to try to analyse what we'd received. And while that actually is a very time-consuming exercise, wastes a lot of time, because it's then almost -- it's not impossible but it's extremely difficult to connect what we analysed to what then comes in in tabbed form. We then, I think like the Chamber, got four volumes and then at the later stage the remaining whatever it is, 13. Ms. Dicklich will correct me on the figures. They came in in tranches, one after the other. And it simply hasn't been possible at the moment to analyse many of or certainly not most of -- untabbed we got on the 28th of April. I'm grateful. Longer ago. It hasn't been possible to analyse many of or most of the untranslated documents, and with the resources available to me it's going to be difficult in the extreme to have any analysis on which to work by the time I start the cross-examination of the witness. And the time, in my submission, has come when this late provision of documents may or must sound in the non-production of exhibits, but can we put it all back, please, until the end of the cross-examination? The Chamber can be quite confident that within the limits of my resources everything is being done to make up for the shortcomings of the presentation by the accused, and either none or very few of these exhibits were mentioned in the 65 ter list either, for what that's worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I make some observations which are material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's material to the evidence that the Trial Chamber is hearing. The accused is charged with Article 7(3), command responsibility. The actions of subordinates within the ministries and the actions of policemen involved in the investigations produce material evidence that are relevant to his criminal liability, and that's one of the big issues that has to be considered by this Court in relation to this material and the individual criminal liability of the accused. So producing materials from the archives through this witness who works at the ministry is a perfectly proper adduction of evidential material before this Trial Chamber. The fact that it is large and voluminous is completely and utterly irrelevant. He is charged with superior responsibility, and that's going to involve large amounts and collections of documents relating to individual crimes out of necessity. He's not an individual charged with hands-on criminal responsibility but for the conduct of subordinates, and that inevitably is going to involve the production and analysis of materials such as this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is very reasonable that everything which relates to the charges of the indictment and the cases relevant to that should be admitted as exhibits. And what Mr. Nice said, that I accumulate material to have them -- and have them translated doubly, the office for the management of documents, which automatically excludes any -- it automatically excludes any document which might appear for translation as an error and be submitted a second time for translation. So the translation service has its own way of preventing such things happening, that is to say a document being tendered twice for translation. Now, as far as the other matter that Mr. Nice brought up here, this is a criminal report that we're dealing with that was filed on the 16th of July, 1998, and which, as far as I can see, in all its facets was compiled pursuant to the provisions. It is indeed an official document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. There are many documents like that among the 143 tabs that you have seen, and all of them, I assume that some of them would be able to indicate any unlawful action on the part of a policeman or someone in the organs of authority in order to confirm that what Mr. Nice says is true. But quite the contrary; all these documents testify to the exact opposite. And the witness is testifying that the police acted contrary to what Mr. Nice said. He even says that there were no criminal acts on the part of the -- that even if certain policemen did engage in criminal acts, steps were taken to prosecute them. So all these stories about the alleged responsibility of the commanders and leaders in the police with respect to the events that are contained in the indictment that I'm charged with is shown not to be correct on the basis of the documents and the testimony of this witness, and therefore all the documents deserve to be introduced into evidence. There could have been many more of them, and there might be many more of them indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As the Chamber had indicated at the beginning of this witness's testimony, questions of admissibility will be decided at the end of the testimony, and that will apply to these documents. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm not going to deal with Racak any more. That is one example of what is contained in paragraph 66. I'm now going to ask you questions with respect to the knowledge of the police or information of the police about the alleged mass grave in Izbica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What paragraph is that of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's paragraph 66(g).

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, before I move on to my specific questions, I'm going to read paragraph 66(g) out to you, which says as follows, and I quote: "On or about the 27th of March, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia shelled the village of Izbica, Srbica municipality, with heavy weapons systems. At least 4.500 villagers from Izbica and surrounding villages took refuge in a meadow in Izbica. On the 28th of March, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded the villagers and approached them, demanding money. After the forces of the FRY and Serbia stole the villagers' valuables, the men were separated from the women and small children. The men were then further divided into two groups, one of which was sent to a nearby hill, and the other was sent to a nearby streambed. The forces of the FRY and Serbia then fired upon both groups of men and at least 116 Kosovo Albanian men were killed." That's the first part. So we have 4.500 villagers set apart, divided into groups. I think there were 116 men, the rest were women and children of the 4.500 villagers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, lay a foundation for the reception of evidence on this matter from this witness. We know he wasn't there. Let him tell us how he came by any information which he's going to provide to us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, what knowledge did you have, what information did the police and you personally have about the alleged mass grave in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was in Pristina myself, and the first news about this alleged grave in the place called Izbica we received or learnt by following on the Internet or some foreign television station. So the first information that reached us, that reached the staff and headquarters of the MUP arrived in the latter part of May 1999, in the third quarter, through aerial photographs that were published over the Internet or which were shown by a foreign television station. Before that, we knew nothing about the event that you have just described. We had absolutely no information and data about it whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means, General, that the police saw this on the Internet. They saw mention of a mass grave in Izbica. That was the first information reaching the police force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what steps did you take following that, then?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with standard police practice, our first task was to check out the information. And in checking out the information, the first step was to find the location that was called that way. And let me say straight away that we spent, I would say, at least seven days, a minimum of seven days, perhaps more, looking for the exact place with that place name. We engaged people who knew the area well. We didn't know what part of Kosovo territory it was located in. All the SUPs, all the staffs were taken up with the business of locating the site. And I know that the journalists accompanied the police in their search. And after a certain amount of time had gone by, we managed to find the particular place, and after we had found the location we continued our normal standard police practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was sent to find the village, then, and to check out the truthfulness of the allegations about this alleged mass grave?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we asked all the SUPs in the territory to see if the place was located on their particular territory, and then it turned out that they thought it was on the territory of the secretariat in Kosovska Mitrovica, and we focused the search on the secretariat of Kosovska Mitrovica, that particular area and that secretariat, because there were indications that the area was there, and a patrol was sent, and after that relatively long period of time, the patrol managed to find the location but they found that it was not the case of a mass grave, as had been alleged, but a freshly dug grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "freshly dug grave," you mean individual graves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean individual graves, relatively new ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, when they found that site, were the crime officials that went there, did they make a record of what they had found?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. And if I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me help you out, General. Was that the Official Note that is found in tab 404?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely that Official Note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what binder is that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is binder 10, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, may we have this Official Note placed on the ELMO. Could you place it on the ELMO, please, General. It's just a short note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, what is the date of that Official Note?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 27th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does the Official Note contain about the source of information about the existence of mass graves -- a mass grave in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning we can see just what I said. The news published on the Internet, in relation to a notice posted on the Internet that, "In the village of Izbica, the SO of Srbica, there is a 'mass grave.' We were dispatched in our capacity as authorised officials to check the veracity of those assertions. For security reasons, when setting out to perform our task, we used a circuitous route across Rudnik, Rakos, and Glina. On our way --" my copy is rather illegible. But it says, "On our way, we --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me help you out there because I have a better copy, it appears. I'm sorry that you were given such a poor copy, photocopy, but this is what it says -- actually, let me ask you the following question: The officials of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, authorised officials ...

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it's important, I can read the contents. I've deciphered what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it says: "In the village itself we met ten soldiers and asked them whether they were -- whether they knew about the existence of a mass grave. They just shrugged their shoulders but they directed us on a downward path to the outskirts of the village where there was a new grave site, cemetery. We passed a large yellow object, and in the region of the last houses to the left, we came upon this cemetery. Judging by the appearance of the graves and grave mounds, the level of the earth covering them, the inscriptions on them with the names of those who had been buried there, and the direction in which the head was pointing, that is to say southward, it was indisputable that this was a Muslim cemetery of recent date. The location itself does not have the appearance of a grave unless there is indeed another place. We emphasise that we did not have the means to obtain more pertinent information from anyone. We left the location in haste because automatic gunfire was heard nearby. Upon our return, we did not see any soldiers in the village." That would be more or less the contents of this Official Note, which explains what I said a moment ago in response to the question I was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the address of the Internet site recorded somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally saw some -- a picture, but it's not contained in the binder. But I have a similar picture about the same event in another village, and perhaps you can see some of that there. I assume it was the same site and the same net, network.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And will we get the Internet site address when we come to that matter? I mean, it's an obvious thing for a policeman to note down, you would think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will receive the photograph and the text, attending text. So there is a copy of the photograph that was shown on the Internet, and it clearly states there Pustocelo [phoen]. It is probably tab 419 or 420, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Mr. Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, were there any locals in the village, any villagers, when the members of the MUP went there with the task of establishing what kind of mass grave it was?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, when they went to check out the situation to see if there was an alleged mass grave, this patrol didn't come across any villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any information about -- just let me take a moment to find this. I have received information from Professor Rakic that on the film which we have but I didn't intend to show because it just shows that the place -- well, what the general said a moment ago. They looked for the place, the journalists looked for the place, and so did the police, and General -- the general said it took them seven days to find the location. Now, the film that was shown by television was -- found one place called Izbica but it doesn't seem to be the same Izbica, and there's a satellite aerial photograph and we'll be able to find that. Mr. Bonomy asked for it, I think, a moment ago. So we'll find a reference to that, its number and so on, the aerial photograph. I don't want to spend time on that just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to the state that the houses in the village were in when the crime investigation team arrived?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not have any precise information to that effect, but I assume there was nothing unusual there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They found a cemetery there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Photographs from that cemetery, are they contained in tab 409? Could you please open tab 409.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is actually a photo file on the location of that cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does this tab contain 16 photographs of the village and the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end there is also a sketch of the cemetery itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. There are photographs of the village in this tab, then photographs of the cemetery, and finally a sketch of the graveyard itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who took those photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, who took these photographs?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The service, the technical service of the police station in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they the ones who compiled this note?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team that was involved was from that service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And when were they taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While carrying out the on-site investigation in Izbica. But that will probably be seen from another tab.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, photocopies are provided in this tab of these photographs of the cemetery, and the visibility is very poor. I have photographs here that are in colour, the actual photographs, and I would like to have them played on the overhead projector, a few photographs from the actual scene, from this tab 409. You can identify them if you compare them to the black and white ones. If you put them on the overhead projector as black and white, you can hardly see them, they're barely discernible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you wish us to see in these colour photographs that we are not seeing in the photographs here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, an expert could probably see all of it in these photographs, too, but it is going to be much clearer on the colour photographs. For example, you will be able to see what is written there. On the black and white ones you cannot see at all what is written. So some you will be able to see the writing on the tombstones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you can show them in any order you wish, these photographs. Oh, black and white again. Ah, yes, it has to be focused.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously this is a close-up of one segment of the cemetery with one of the tombstones, where it clearly says -- where you can clearly see what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to draw your attention to the date. Could you please read out the date.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, the 11th of May, 1999. Again this is a close-up of one particular grave. The only thing I can read here is the abbreviation UCK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can it be focused a bit? Can you see the date here?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally cannot see it. Oh, but in all fairness, the 10th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 10th of May, 1999. I can read it myself. I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me which -- can you tell me which photograph in the binder that is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me, Mr. Bonomy, that that is on photograph 14, except that what we are seeing is a close-up of this board that was like a tombstone, like the previous one on number 13, but we can compare them, we can compare the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But they don't look the same photographs to me, unless we're seeing only a restricted part of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, only a part, of course, because we are viewing a close-up now. Well, now on the projector you can't see anything. Everything has gone dark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this black and white photograph, number 14, I can see the abbreviation on the top of the tombstone. But obviously this is a photograph of the same spot but it is a close-up rather than taken from a distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The abbreviation I see are in much bolder letters than the rest of the writing, the abbreviation UCK. Would there be any significance to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is of significance is that UCK is inscribed there. It certainly was not done by the policemen. It must have been somebody else. And then there's the date, the 10th of May, 1999. On photograph number 14 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My photograph 14 has a cone with a number 4 on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These numbers 4 and 3, I assume, are the numbers that were placed there by the forensic technicians when they were actually taking the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is it in the photograph on the screen if that's number 14?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I'm not saying it's the same photograph. I'm saying it's a photograph of the same object at the same locality. If you have any doubts as to whether it's the same place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we're now looking at photographs of which we don't have copies, and as long as I know that, then it would save me wasting time looking at the copies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will try to establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, part of the difficulty here is that the witness can't help very much. He never visited the site.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the witness clearly said when they found out via the Internet that there was a new mass grave near Pristina, he explained what a great effort they made to find the locality in order to establish what was actually there, because regardless of who they receive information from, the police are supposed to check it out. In this case, they got from satellite a piece of information that was actually broadcast by NATO. It doesn't matter who broadcast it. What matters is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I have stopped you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that this witness is saying anything about this photograph or is in any position to do so. The photographs were produced by the accused and that's all we know about them. I'm doing the best I can to help. I'm looking at Schedule F in the indictment, if that's what the accused is concerned about, to see if I can connect the name on the gravestone, wherever it may be found, to the name in that schedule, and I can't find it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, on my understanding, the witness is telling us that these are official photographs, and unfortunately that perfectly straightforward evidence is being undermined by confusion over what photographs we're actually looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course if the witness is able to say that he produces them, knows where they came from, and can testify to all those matters, fine. But as it looks, they came from the accused's hand, were additional to the photographs in the exhibit that the witness did produce, and as far as I can see, don't specifically relate to the issue in hand, which is Schedule F of the indictment. That's as far as I can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, please be so kind as to look at the back of these photographs that you have. Please look at the back of these photographs. Is there anything there? Are there any markings there? What is that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the seal of the Secretariat of the Interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Republican Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So that is the stamp of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the ministry -- it's easier for me to read it on this screen. The republic of Serbia, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Belgrade, and of course a number too. The Roman numeral, I assume, denotes the organisational unit involved, that is to say, the Secretariat of the Interior in Mitrovica. Of course I'm not sure. But the stamp of every secretariat bears the wording "ministry" within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the rest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this should be your last question before we break for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, General. This stamp of the ministry, does it show that this is part of the official documentation concerning the locality that can be seen here?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This stamp would have to mean that this -- these photographs were developed by some unit from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you something, to establish something that's not very difficult for you. If you look at the number, will you establish what secretariat this is? You can check it out, can you not?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it cannot -- it can be checked, but of course at this point in time I cannot say whose exact number this is. As far as I can see, the number is 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have to conclude today's evidence. We will adjourn until Wednesday of next week, 9.00 a.m. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of May, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
